articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations for Narcotics and Terrorism
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting several Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations (DTOs) for their involvement in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. The designated entities include 'LOS LORENZANAS' (also known as the LORENZANA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, 'THE LORENZANA CLAN,' and 'THE LORENZANA FAMILY'), 'LOS MENDOZA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION,' and 'LOS HUISTAS DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION'.

These organizations have been added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List, with 'LOS LORENZANAS' identified as a Transnational Terrorist Group and Criminal Organization. The designations carry secondary sanctions risk under section 1(b) of Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886. The 'LOS MENDOZA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION' is linked to the SINALOA CARTEL, and 'LOS HUISTAS DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION' is linked to both the SINALOA CARTEL and the CARTEL DE JALISCO NUEVA GENERACION.

The action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to disrupt the financial networks of criminal organizations that pose a threat to international security. These designations aim to sever their access to the U.S. financial system and impede their ability to conduct illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This update is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to address threats posed by the Iranian regime.

While specific details of the designations were not immediately released in a separate press statement, such updates typically involve adding individuals or entities to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List or other sanctions lists. These actions aim to further restrict the Iranian government's access to the international financial system and its ability to fund destabilizing activities.
The update follows a series of Iran-related designations and alerts issued by OFAC in recent weeks, indicating a continued focus on Iranian sanctions enforcement.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Iran-related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These designations are part of the ongoing pressure campaign against the Iranian regime and its illicit activities.

The specific individuals and entities targeted by these designations were not detailed in the initial announcement but are expected to be added to OFAC's sanctions lists, thereby blocking their assets and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with them.
This action reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to countering Iran's proliferation of weapons, support for terrorism, and human rights abuses through economic sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a multifaceted sanctions action on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new designations related to Cuba. OFAC also published a Cuba-related Determination pursuant to Section 2(a)(i)(A) of Executive Order 14404, specifically identifying the 'Electronics, Manufacturing, Marine, and Technology Sectors of the Cuban Economy' as subject to sanctions.

Among the entities added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List are those involved in global scam networks and the corporate infrastructure enabling them. For Cuba, the designations include EMPRESA COMERCIALIZADORA DE SERVICIOS TECNICOS Y TECNOLOGICOS (TECNOSIME) and EMPRESA IMPORTADORA Y EXPORTADORA DE PRODUCTOS DE LA ELECTRONICA Y LAS COMUNICACIONES (CUBAELECTRONICA), both identified as Cuban state-owned enterprises. This expands the scope of sanctions beyond the five sectors initially named in E.O. 14404.

This action aims to disrupt illicit financial activities globally and further pressure the Cuban regime by targeting key economic sectors that generate revenue for the government. U.S. importers, exporters, carriers, and logistics providers are advised to re-screen foreign suppliers, vessels, and customers with any Cuba connection in these newly identified sectors.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations, Issues Alert on 'Shadow Fleet,' and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings, the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert, and the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License and Frequently Asked Question.

The Iran-related Alert, titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion,' highlights the significant risk of designation or penalties for providing services to vessels using false flags to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran. OFAC specifically targeted individuals and entities involved in operating fraudulent ship registries, including Ashwani Kumar Dhiman, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, Suniel Kumar Sharma, and several India-based companies such as ARYAVART SHIP MANAGEMENT PRIVATE LIMITED and POLYNESIA MARITIME PRIVATE LIMITED, all linked to Iran's 'shadow fleet' and carrying secondary sanctions risk.

Additionally, OFAC issued Venezuela-related General License 5AA, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or After December 18, 2026,' and amended FAQ 595. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' a broader initiative to disrupt the Iranian regime's revenue channels.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced on October 29, 2026, the issuance of Iran General License FF-1. This General License, titled 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance,' facilitates the orderly cessation of certain financial activities.

This action provides a specific authorization for U.S. persons to wind down transactions that were previously permissible but are now impacted by sanctions. Such general licenses are crucial for ensuring that businesses and individuals can comply with sanctions regulations while minimizing disruption to legitimate activities.

The issuance of General License FF-1 follows a pattern of OFAC providing clear guidance and wind-down periods for transactions affected by new or amended sanctions, allowing for a structured exit from prohibited dealings.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals for North Korea and DRC Sanctions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in activities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and address destabilizing activities in both regions.

For North Korea, the designations include Russian and North Korean nationals linked to entities such as LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER, with some entries listing digital wallets on Ethereum and TRON. These individuals and entities are accused of facilitating illicit financial transactions for the DPRK, including for Amnokgang Technology Development Company.

In relation to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, OFAC designated Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and the Zigama Credit and Savings Society (also known as Zigama CSS), a Kigali-based financial institution. These designations were made under E.O. 13413 for supporting the M23 armed group and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance, in eastern DRC. The new designations increase secondary sanctions risks for financial institutions engaging in transactions with these regions.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement on October 27, 2026, with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-headquartered cloud networking solutions provider. Extreme Networks agreed to pay $1,529,685 to resolve apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services on nine occasions from the United States to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to being majority-owned by the designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, citing Extreme Networks' reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and failure to conduct sufficient due diligence. A parallel non-prosecution agreement was reached with the Department of Justice, with a portion of the OFAC settlement potentially satisfied by payments under the DOJ agreement.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced on October 26, 2026, amendments to several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of OFAC's ongoing review process to ensure its published guidance remains current and clear.

The revised FAQs, specifically numbers 10, 32 through 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, address various aspects of sanctions compliance. These include clarifying which jurisdictions are subject to broad sanctions, how to block an account or funds transfer, the interest required on blocked funds, and when to reject rather than block a transaction.

The amendments also provide clearer guidance on notification to customers when property is blocked, account openings and transactions involving blocked persons, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions through the OFAC Reporting System. These updates are crucial for financial institutions and businesses to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of actions on October 21, 2026, including new Iran-related designations, removals of certain Belarus and North Korea designations, and the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations target entities and individuals involved in activities that support the Iranian regime's destabilizing actions. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a dynamic approach to sanctions policy based on evolving geopolitical considerations.

The issuance of new General Licenses for Iran and Russia, along with amended FAQs, aims to provide clarity and authorization for specific types of transactions, ensuring that legitimate humanitarian and other permitted activities can continue while maintaining the integrity of sanctions regimes.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has paid a civil penalty of $1,529,685 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. The settlement addresses nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and related services to a Russian defense manufacturer that was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by a designated entity. OFAC determined that these violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious.

This penalty underscores the importance of thorough due diligence and robust compliance programs, especially when dealing with entities that may be indirectly owned or controlled by sanctioned parties.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Assessed $11,662,930 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This significant penalty highlights the critical need for financial institutions to maintain stringent sanctions compliance programs.

While the specific details of the violations leading to this penalty were not immediately available in the public record, OFAC civil penalties typically arise from failures to block prohibited transactions, process transactions involving sanctioned parties, or report blocked property in a timely and accurate manner.
This enforcement action serves as a reminder to all financial institutions of their obligations under U.S. sanctions laws and the substantial consequences of non-compliance.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 in OFAC Civil Penalty
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has paid a civil penalty of $175,015 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty addresses apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations.

Logistics companies play a crucial role in international trade and are therefore subject to OFAC's regulations, particularly concerning the movement of goods to or from sanctioned jurisdictions or involving sanctioned parties. Failures in screening or due diligence can lead to significant penalties.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding companies accountable for ensuring that their operations do not facilitate transactions that violate U.S. sanctions policy.

articles.headline: Individual Assessed $1,427,230 OFAC Civil Penalty
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. This substantial penalty highlights that individuals, not just corporations, are subject to significant enforcement actions for sanctions breaches.

OFAC's enforcement against individuals often involves facilitating prohibited transactions, engaging in dealings with sanctioned entities, or attempting to evade sanctions. The specific details of the individual's violations were not immediately available.
This action serves as a strong deterrent, emphasizing that personal involvement in sanctions evasion or violations carries severe financial consequences.

articles.headline: Global Central Banks Eye Inflation Trends Amidst Mixed Economic Signals
body: Central banks worldwide are closely monitoring inflation trends as they navigate a landscape of mixed economic signals. While some regions show signs of moderating price increases, others continue to grapple with persistent inflationary pressures, complicating monetary policy decisions. The Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, and Bank of England are all expected to maintain a cautious stance, emphasizing data-dependency in their upcoming policy meetings.

Energy prices, particularly for oil and natural gas, remain a significant factor influencing inflation, with geopolitical tensions contributing to volatility. Supply chain improvements have offered some relief, but labor market tightness in several major economies continues to exert upward pressure on wages and, consequently, consumer prices.

Analysts anticipate that central banks will likely hold interest rates steady in the near term, allowing previous rate hikes to fully transmit through the economy. However, the possibility of further tightening remains on the table if inflation proves more stubborn than expected, or if new economic shocks emerge.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced last week that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List. This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of these newly controlled items, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

Jeffrey I. Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, stated that this move is a 'common-sense action that alleviates the compliance burden on America's proud firearms industry, while continuing to protect national security.'

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
